raw_response:
I've been farming these 6 mu in Quzhou for 30 years, and at 60, I know every slight variation in the soil across my small plot. With my agricultural college background, I understand the county extension recommendations well, but I've also learned that on a 6-mu farm with three mouths to feed, you can't simply follow the textbook — you have to balance agronomic targets against cash flow and survival. I don't chase maximum yield; I chase consistent, reasonable returns with managed risk.

For winter wheat, I'll plant the full 6 mu in mid-October. I'm using an improved semi-dwarf variety — not the newest hybrid on the market, but a proven performer that gives me about 450 kg/mu in a normal year. Seed rate is 7.5 kg/mu, running roughly 40 yuan/mu. For fertility, I'm targeting that 450 kg/mu yield based on my soil conditions and last year's performance. I'll apply 50 kg/mu of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) as a base before planting — that gives me about 7.5 kg each of N, P, and K per mu. Then at jointing stage in late March, I'll topdress 15 kg/mu of urea, adding another 7 kg N. Total nitrogen comes to about 14.5 kg/mu. The extension station recommends 18–20 kg N for high-yield targets, but I've found through years of trials that 14–15 kg is the efficient point on my land, and saving that 60 yuan per mu matters when my total cash for inputs is tight.

For irrigation, I'll run water three times: winter irrigation in late November to protect against winter kill, jointing irrigation in March, and heading irrigation in mid-April. If May brings decent rainfall, I'll skip grain-filling irrigation to save on pumping — each pass costs me about 30 yuan per mu, and on 6 mu that adds up to real money. For crop protection, I'll apply a pre-emergence herbicide on the wheat, but I don't spray fungicide preventively; I scout first.

Come mid-June, the wheat comes off and summer maize goes in within three to four days. The turnaround is brutally tight, so there's no time for deep tillage. I'll use minimal tillage and direct seeding with a hybrid maize variety. Hybrid seed costs about 70 yuan per mu, but the yield gain over saved seed is worth it — I expect about 500 kg/mu if the weather cooperates. For fertilizer, I'll put down 40 kg/mu of compound at planting and side-dress 10 kg/mu of urea at the V6–V8 stage. That totals about 12 kg N/mu, which is slightly below the extension recommendation but appropriate for my rotation and soil fertility buildup over the years. Maize gets two irrigations: one at around V8 and one at tasseling in late July or early August. I'll add a third only if August turns dry, because electricity for pumping is metered and costly.

For pest management on maize, I'll apply herbicide at planting, and I'll scout for corn borer weekly during July. If I see egg masses or early damage, I'll spray insecticide, but I won't spray blindly — that's cash I can't afford to waste.

Labor is mostly family. With three of us in the household, we can handle planting, fertilizing, irrigating, and most of the harvest. But wheat harvest and maize planting fall in the same week in June, and at my age I can't work 16-hour days in that heat. I'll hire labor for 2 days during wheat harvest and 3 days for the maize planting push. Day labor is running about 150 yuan per day now, which stings, but missing the planting window would cost me far more.

My total input budget this year is about 4,600 yuan. That leaves me with a cash cushion for emergencies — my wife's medicine, equipment repairs, or a sudden irrigation need if a drought hits. At 60, I've seen too many farmers go broke chasing one big year. Slow and steady is how I've kept this land for three decades.
